displayQuote: The man who dies thus rich dies disgraced

meta.title: Who really said "The man who dies thus rich dies disgraced"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Verified: Carnegie wrote it on p. 664 of “Wealth,” North American Review, June 1889 — but the famous short form drops his word “thus,” and he disowned that.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The man who dies thus rich dies disgraced'?
meta.ogDescription: Real, and in print: “Wealth,” North American Review, June 1889, p. 664. The popular short version drops Carnegie’s word “thus” — and he denied saying it.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Carnegie wrote this exact sentence — “thus” and all — on page 664 of Wealth, his essay in The North American Review of June 1889 ↗, where it lands as the second-to-last line of the argument. Worth noticing how he frames it: the words sit inside quotation marks as “the public verdict” he expects a future generation to pronounce, not as a motto he is issuing in his own voice.

source.heading: Where it actually appears

source.excerpt: This day already dawns. But a little while, and although, without incurring the pity of their fellows, men may die sharers in great business enterprises from which their capital cannot be or has not been withdrawn, and is left chiefly at death for public uses, yet the man who dies leaving behind him millions of available wealth, which was his to administer during life, will pass away “unwept, unhonored, and unsung,” no matter to what uses he leaves the dross which he cannot take with him. Of such as these the public verdict will then be: “The man who dies thus rich dies disgraced.”
trail: Read the sentence in a transcription proofread against the original page images: Wikisource’s text of “Wealth” ↗, where the running head on the relevant page reads 664 · WEALTH · THE NORTH AMERICAN REVIEW.
Cross-checked the citation against Wikiquote’s Andrew Carnegie page ↗, which lists the line under Wealth, 1889 with North American Review vol. 148, issue 391, pp. 653–664 and places it on p. 664.
Confirmed the full “thus” wording is the one Carnegie’s own foundation quotes, on the Carnegie Corporation of New York’s Gospel of Wealth page ↗.
Traced the popular short form and Carnegie’s objection to it through the American Dialect Society archive ↗, which reproduces the Washington Post Q&A of 11 March 1906, p. 11, col. 6.
source.excerptNote: The quotation marks are Carnegie’s own. He is not declaring the verdict — he is forecasting it, and the word thus ties it to the specific man described in the preceding clause.

author.name: Andrew Carnegie
author.heading: Andrew Carnegie
author.bio: Born in Dunfermline, Fife, in 1835 and taken to Pennsylvania as a boy, Carnegie built the steel empire that made him one of the richest men alive, then spent the rest of his life trying to get rid of the money. Wikipedia records that he gave away roughly $350 million — almost 90 percent of his fortune — in the last eighteen years of his life, funding some 3,000 libraries across the United States and a dozen other countries. He died in 1919, which is the detail that makes this quote unusual among rich men’s epigrams: he actually did the thing he said.

misattribution.heading: The famous version is not quite the real one
misattribution.intro: This is that rare case where the quote is genuine and the popular quote is not. The line everyone repeats is one word shorter than the line Carnegie wrote — and when it was credited to a speech rather than to his essay, Carnegie put his denial in writing.

items.who: “The man who dies rich dies disgraced”
items.why: The circulating short form drops thus, and the word was doing real work. In the essay it points back to the man Carnegie has just described in the same sentence — one who dies “leaving behind him millions of available wealth, which was his to administer during life.” Without it the sentence reads as a blanket condemnation of dying wealthy, which is not the claim. Quote sites carry the trimmed version with no source attached at all, as on Goodreads ↗, where it is displayed as “The man who dies rich, dies disgraced.”

The Washington Post’s Questions and Answers column of 11 March 1906 was asked when Carnegie made his famous epigram, and answered that the phrase had been credited to a library-commission dinner in Pittsburgh in 1894 — but that Carnegie denied it in a letter written when the phrase first gained currency: “What I have said about wealth is found in my own writings, and not in extracts from supposed speeches.” The column is reproduced in the American Dialect Society archive ↗.

The same archived posting observes that Bartlett’s carries the quotation and dates it to Carnegie in 1889 without footnoting his denial, and that The American Heritage Dictionary of American Quotations omits it entirely. The 1889 date is right; what gets lost is that Carnegie objected to the version people actually repeat. See the archived note ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence is genuinely Carnegie’s — look for it in print, not at a podium: Wealth, The North American Review, June 1889 ↗, p. 664, where it reads “The man who dies thus rich dies disgraced.”

context.heading: Why he wrote it
lead: Carnegie’s 1889 essay is not a sermon about generosity. It is a piece of hard-headed self-interest addressed to his own class: give the surplus away yourself, deliberately and while you are alive, or watch it be dispersed by heirs who did not earn it, by the tax collector, or by a public that has run out of patience. The famous line is the stick at the end of the argument — the reputational cost he predicts for anyone who ignores it.

The essay ran in The North American Review under the plain title “Wealth.” Wikipedia records that after William Ewart Gladstone read it, a British edition followed in The Pall Mall Gazette under the heading it has carried ever since: The Gospel of Wealth ↗. Carnegie himself only used the phrase in passing, in the sentence immediately after the famous one.
detailsBody: Read on one line past the famous verdict and you get Carnegie’s own label for the whole doctrine: “Such, in my opinion, is the true Gospel concerning Wealth, obedience to which is destined some day to solve the problem of the Rich and the Poor.” The essay then closes on a borrowed phrase — “Peace on earth, among men Good-Will” — and Carnegie’s printed signature.
context.pull: He put it in quotation marks because he was not making a declaration — he was predicting an epitaph.

sourcesVerified.claim: Carnegie's essay "Wealth" contains verbatim: 'Of such as these the public verdict will then be: "The man who dies thus rich dies disgraced."' immediately followed by 'Such, in my opinion, is the true Gospel concerning Wealth...' and ending 'Peace on earth, among men Good-Will.'
The page bearing the quoted sentence carries the running head '664 / WEALTH / THE NORTH AMERICAN REVIEW' and ends with the printed signature 'Andrew Carnegie.'

Wikiquote lists 'The man who dies thus rich dies disgraced.' under the section 'Wealth, 1889' with the citation North American Review, June 1889, vol. 148, issue 391, p. 653-664, and places the quote at p. 664.

Carnegie Corporation of New York describes The Gospel of Wealth as a pair of articles first published in the North American Review in 1889 and quotes the declaration 'The man who dies thus rich dies disgraced.'

The Washington Post Questions and Answers column of 11 March 1906, p. 11, col. 6, states the circulating form is 'the man who dies rich dies disgraced', that the phrase was attributed to a library-commission dinner in Pittsburgh in 1894, and quotes Carnegie's letter: 'What I have said about wealth is found in my own writings, and not in extracts from supposed speeches.' The same posting notes Bartlett's attributes it to Carnegie in 1889 without footnoting the denial, and that the American Heritage Dictionary of American Quotations omits it.

The essay was originally titled 'Wealth' and published in the North American Review in June 1889; it was later published as 'The Gospel of Wealth' in The Pall Mall Gazette; the book The Gospel of Wealth and Other Timely Essays was published in 1901 by Century.

Andrew Carnegie was born 25 November 1835 in Dunfermline, Fife, Scotland, died 11 August 1919, is described as a Scottish-American industrialist and philanthropist, gave away about $350 million (almost 90 percent of his fortune) in the last 18 years of his life, funded approximately 3,000 libraries, and published 'Wealth' in the North American Review in 1889, which appeared in Britain as 'The Gospel of Wealth' in The Pall Mall Gazette after Gladstone read it.
The Internet Archive hosts a scan of Andrew Carnegie's 'Wealth' from the North American Review, June 1889, pp. 653-664, as a public-domain work.
Goodreads displays the quote in the shortened form 'The man who dies rich, dies disgraced.' attributed to Andrew Carnegie with no source work cited.
Quote Investigator has no article covering this quotation (site search for 'dies rich dies disgraced' returns Nothing Found), so no QI anchor exists to defer to.
